ruleExplorerChemistry.title: Combustion Conditions (Fire Triangle)
ruleExplorerChemistry.instructions: Toggle Fuel, Oxygen, and Sufficient Heat to test when ordinary combustion can occur.
ruleExplorerChemistry.fallbackText: In the fire triangle model, ordinary combustion requires fuel, oxygen and sufficient heat to initiate and sustain burning.

codePlaygroundPython.title: Python Pass/Retry Check
codePlaygroundPython.instructions: Run the Python snippet and test normal and boundary marks (49, 50, 51, 0, and 100).
codePlaygroundPython.fallbackText: When mark >= 50 the program prints Pass; otherwise it prints Retry (boundary values: 49 -> Retry, 50 -> Pass, 51 -> Pass).

codePlaygroundPseudocode.title: Cambridge Pseudocode Accumulator Loop
codePlaygroundPseudocode.instructions: Run the examination-standard Cambridge pseudocode FOR loop with explicit INTEGER declarations to compute the sum of 1 to 5.
codePlaygroundPseudocode.fallbackText: Declaring Total and Count as INTEGER and summing 1 through 5 in a FOR loop outputs 15.
codePlaygroundPseudocode.pseudocodeStarter:
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
Total ← 0
FOR Count ← 1 TO 5
    Total ← Total + Count
NEXT Count
OUTPUT Total

codePlaygroundSql.title: Read-Only Stock Filter Query
codePlaygroundSql.instructions: Run the SELECT query against the isolated Stock table (Pen, Ruler, Book, Bag, Pencil) to list items with Quantity < 6 ordered by Price descending.
codePlaygroundSql.fallbackText: Against GAM EDU's Stock fixture, SELECT ItemName, Price FROM Stock WHERE Quantity < 6 ORDER BY Price DESC returns 3 rows: Bag (35), Ruler (4), and Pencil (1.5). Pen (Qty 12) and Book (Qty 20) are excluded.
codePlaygroundSql.sqlStarter:
SELECT ItemName, Price
FROM Stock
WHERE Quantity < 6
ORDER BY Price DESC;

constructionLabBooleanCircuit.title: Boolean Circuit Challenge: A AND (NOT B)
constructionLabBooleanCircuit.instructions: Construct a circuit that produces an output of 1 only when input A is 1 and input B is 0. Test all four possible input combinations and verify your circuit using a truth table.
constructionLabBooleanCircuit.fallbackText: Connect input B through a NOT gate, then feed input A and (NOT B) into an AND gate. The output is 1 only when A=1 and B=0.

pilot4a-math-quadratic.title: Discover Quadratic Vertex Form
pilot4a-math-quadratic.instructions: Move a, h, and k to see how the vertex (h, k) and curvature compare with the reference parabola y = x².
pilot4a-math-quadratic.accessibilityLabel: Quadratic vertex form graph and parameter sliders
pilot4a-math-quadratic.fallbackText: In y = a(x - h)^2 + k, when a ≠ 0 the vertex sits at (h, k), negative a flips the parabola downward, and |a| > 1 narrows it; when a = 0, the graph becomes the horizontal constant function y = k (not a parabola).
pilot4a-math-quadratic.modelNote: Real-valued function y = a(x - h)^2 + k plotted over x in [-6, 6]. Note: when a = 0, y = k is a horizontal constant function rather than a parabola.

challenges.prompt: Make the parabola open downward (a < 0) with its vertex at (2, 4).
challenges.successText: Well done! Because a < 0, the vertex (2, 4) is a maximum point.
challenges.hintText: Set a to a negative value, h = 2, and k = 4.

pilot4a-phys-projectile.title: Discover Projectile Motion
pilot4a-phys-projectile.instructions: Adjust launch angle and initial speed to observe how the trajectory, range, and maximum height respond.
pilot4a-phys-projectile.accessibilityLabel: Projectile motion trajectory graph and sliders
pilot4a-phys-projectile.fallbackText: With constant g = 9.81 m/s² and no air resistance on level ground, horizontal range is maximised at 45° and complementary angles (30° and 60°) yield equal range.
pilot4a-phys-projectile.modelNote: Idealised projectile motion: g = 9.81 m/s², no air resistance, equal launch and landing heights.

challenges.prompt: Keep initial speed at 26 m/s and set the launch angle that gives the greatest horizontal range.
challenges.successText: Exact! At θ = 45° and v₀ = 26 m/s, sin(2θ) = 1, giving the maximum range of 68.91 m.
challenges.hintText: Make sure initial speed stays at 26 m/s and compare 30°, 45°, and 60°.

pilot4a-phys-ohms-law.title: How Does Resistance Affect Current?
pilot4a-phys-ohms-law.instructions: Compare the current-voltage graph for your chosen resistance R against the dashed 3 Ω reference resistor.
pilot4a-phys-ohms-law.accessibilityLabel: Ohm's Law current versus voltage graph and sliders
pilot4a-phys-ohms-law.fallbackText: By Ohm's Law (I = V / R), keeping voltage at 6 V and doubling resistance from 3 Ω to 6 Ω halves the current from 2.00 A to 1.00 A.
pilot4a-phys-ohms-law.modelNote: Ideal ohmic resistor with constant resistance at each setting.

prediction.prompt: A circuit has V = 6 V and R = 3 Ω (current = 2 A). What happens to current if resistance doubles to 6 Ω at constant 6 V?
prediction.explanation: Current is inversely proportional to resistance (I = V / R), so doubling R halves I.

challenges.prompt: Set Test Voltage to 6 V and Resistance to 6 Ω to confirm the current drops to 1.00 A.
challenges.successText: Confirmed! At 6 V and 6 Ω, I = 6 / 6 = 1.00 A — half the original 2.00 A.
challenges.hintText: Set Test Voltage = 6 V and Resistance = 6 Ω.

pilot4a-sci-wave.title: Discover the Properties of a Transverse Wave
pilot4a-sci-wave.instructions: Vary Amplitude (A), Wavelength (λ), and Frequency (f) to observe the spatial wave snapshot and calculated wave speed.
pilot4a-sci-wave.accessibilityLabel: Transverse wave spatial snapshot graph and sliders
pilot4a-sci-wave.fallbackText: In a spatial wave snapshot y(x) = A sin(2πx / λ), amplitude A sets peak height, wavelength λ sets crest-to-crest distance, wave speed is v = fλ, and period is T = 1/f.
pilot4a-sci-wave.modelNote: Spatial displacement snapshot y(x) at a fixed instant in time (distinct from a displacement-time graph y(t)). In a fixed-speed medium, f and λ are inversely related (v constant); here, f and λ can be varied independently to show how wave speed v = fλ and period T = 1/f respond while the frozen spatial shape depends only on A and λ.

challenges.prompt: Double the amplitude to 2 m while keeping wavelength at 2 m. Notice the crests stay 2 m apart.
challenges.successText: Exactly! Increasing amplitude makes the wave taller without changing its wavelength.
challenges.hintText: Set Amplitude = 2 m and keep Wavelength = 2 m.

pilot4a-econ-equilibrium.title: Explore Market Equilibrium
pilot4a-econ-equilibrium.instructions: Adjust the demand and supply intercepts to watch the intersection point and equilibrium readouts shift.
pilot4a-econ-equilibrium.accessibilityLabel: Supply and demand market equilibrium graph
pilot4a-econ-equilibrium.fallbackText: For linear curves P_d = d₀ - Q and P_s = s₀ + Q, equilibrium occurs at Q* = (d₀ - s₀)/2 and P* = (d₀ + s₀)/2.
pilot4a-econ-equilibrium.modelNote: Simplified linear market model with all other market conditions held constant (ceteris paribus).

challenges.prompt: Hold Supply intercept at 20 GH₵ and raise Demand intercept to 100 GH₵. Confirm equilibrium price reaches 60 GH₵.
challenges.successText: Correct! With stronger demand (d₀ = 100) and unchanged supply (s₀ = 20), P* rises from 50 to 60 GH₵ and Q* rises from 30 to 40 units.
challenges.hintText: Keep Supply = 20 GH₵ and move Demand to 100 GH₵.

pilot4a-sci-distance-time.title: Piecewise Distance–Time Journey
pilot4a-sci-distance-time.instructions: Scrub the coordinate inspector across 0 to 10 seconds and open the data table to compare speeds in each stage.
pilot4a-sci-distance-time.accessibilityLabel: Piecewise distance-time graph of a three-stage journey
pilot4a-sci-distance-time.fallbackText: Stage 1 (0–4 s): 40 m at 10 m/s. Stage 2 (4–7 s): stationary at 40 m (0 m/s). Stage 3 (7–10 s): 60 m in 3 s (20 m/s).
pilot4a-sci-distance-time.modelNote: Declarative piecewise linear segments (no executable conditions).

pilot4a-math-discontinuity.title: Asymptote & Discontinuity Explorer
pilot4a-math-discontinuity.instructions: Adjust k to scale y = k / x and inspect how both y = k / x and y = tan(x) break cleanly across asymptotes.
pilot4a-math-discontinuity.accessibilityLabel: Reciprocal and tangent function discontinuity graph
pilot4a-math-discontinuity.fallbackText: y = k / x is undefined at x = 0; y = tan(x) is undefined at odd multiples of π/2 (~ ±1.57). Branches do not connect across asymptotes.
pilot4a-math-discontinuity.modelNote: Angles for tan(x) are in radians; SVG clipPath prevents false horizontal clamping.

pilot4a-cs-digital-step.title: Digital Signal Step-Line Waveform
pilot4a-cs-digital-step.instructions: Use the time inspector to read the discrete binary state (0 = LOW, 1 = HIGH) at each clock interval.
pilot4a-cs-digital-step.accessibilityLabel: Digital signal binary step waveform graph
pilot4a-cs-digital-step.fallbackText: Binary sequence 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0 switches cleanly between 0 (LOW) and 1 (HIGH) at clock edges.
pilot4a-cs-digital-step.modelNote: Declarative step-line series (kind='step') — zero diagonal interpolation.

pilot4b-bio-mitosis.title: Mitosis and the Cell Division Process
pilot4b-bio-mitosis.instructions: Step through all six stages for a model diploid cell (2n = 4) and track how DNA, chromatids, and the nuclear membrane change.
pilot4b-bio-mitosis.accessibilityLabel: Interactive six-stage mitosis and cell division stepper
pilot4b-bio-mitosis.fallbackText: Interphase replicates DNA before mitosis. Prophase condenses chromosomes, Metaphase aligns them at the equator, Anaphase separates sister chromatids, Telophase reforms nuclei, and Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm into two identical 2n = 4 daughter cells.
pilot4b-bio-mitosis.modelNote: Interphase precedes mitosis; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and may overlap late mitosis. Model diploid count: 2n = 4.

stages.title: Interphase (Preparation)
stages.summary: Before mitosis begins, the cell grows and replicates its DNA during S phase so each of the 4 chromosomes consists of two identical sister chromatids.
stages.startingCondition: 4 unreplicated chromosomes (4 chromatids) inside an intact nucleus.
stages.whatChanges: DNA replicates; chromatid count doubles from 4 to 8 while chromosome count stays 4.
stages.whyItMatters: Guarantees both daughter cells inherit an exact, complete copy of the genome.
stages.connectionToNext: Once DNA replication and growth checkpoints pass, the cell enters Prophase.
stages.commonMisconception: Interphase is NOT a stage of mitosis—it prepares the cell before mitosis starts.

stages.title: Prophase
stages.summary: Chromatin condenses into visible X-shaped chromosomes (each with two sister chromatids), spindle fibres form, and the nuclear membrane breaks down.
stages.whatChanges: Chromosomes thicken and become visible; nuclear membrane disintegrates.
stages.whyItMatters: Condensing DNA prevents tangling or breaking during movement.
stages.connectionToNext: Spindle fibres attach to centromeres to guide chromosomes to the equator.

stages.title: Metaphase
stages.summary: Spindle fibres align all 4 chromosomes single-file along the cell equator (metaphase plate).
stages.whatChanges: Chromosomes line up centrally with spindle fibres attached to opposite sides of each centromere.
stages.whyItMatters: Ensures each pole receives exactly one sister chromatid from every chromosome.
stages.connectionToNext: Once alignment is checked, centromeres split to start Anaphase.

prediction.prompt: What happens immediately after chromosomes align at the cell equator?
options: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
The nuclear membrane thickens around the equator
prediction.explanation: In Anaphase, centromeres divide and spindle fibres pull sister chromatids to opposite poles.

stages.title: Anaphase
stages.summary: Centromeres split and shortening spindle fibres pull sister chromatids to opposite poles; each separated chromatid is now an individual chromosome.
stages.whatChanges: 4 chromosomes move to the left pole and 4 identical chromosomes move to the right pole.
stages.whyItMatters: Physically divides the duplicated genetic material equally.
stages.connectionToNext: When chromosomes arrive at the poles, Telophase begins.

stages.title: Telophase
stages.summary: Two new nuclear membranes form around the two clusters of 4 chromosomes, which decondense back into chromatin.
stages.whatChanges: Nuclear division (mitosis) completes; two genetically identical nuclei exist in one cell.
stages.connectionToNext: Cytokinesis (which often starts during late telophase) separates the cytoplasm.

stages.title: Cytokinesis
stages.summary: The cytoplasm divides (cleavage furrow in animals; cell plate in plants), producing two separate, genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
stages.whatChanges: One parent cell becomes two independent daughter cells.
stages.whyItMatters: Completes cell division for growth and tissue repair.

sequenceChallenge.prompt: Arrange the four core phases of mitosis (nuclear division) in the correct order.
sequenceChallenge.explanation: Nuclear division follows PMAT: Prophase (condense) → Metaphase (align) → Anaphase (separate) → Telophase (reform nuclei).

pilot4b-cs-fde-cycle.title: CPU Fetch–Decode–Execute Cycle (Example: LOAD 5)
pilot4b-cs-fde-cycle.instructions: Step through the registers as the CPU executes LOAD 5 (stored at address 100, where memory[5] holds value 42).
pilot4b-cs-fde-cycle.accessibilityLabel: Interactive CPU Fetch Decode Execute register stepper
pilot4b-cs-fde-cycle.fallbackText: PC (100) copies to MAR; memory[100] ('LOAD 5') loads into MDR then CIR; PC increments to 101; Control Unit decodes LOAD 5; Execute reads memory[5] (42) into ACC.
pilot4b-cs-fde-cycle.modelNote: Simplified single-accumulator Von Neumann model executing LOAD 5. Not all instructions pass through the ALU (LOAD transfers memory to ACC directly). Restarting the cycle replays this LOAD 5 example rather than fetching address 101.

stages.title: Fetch 1: Copy PC to MAR
stages.summary: The address of the next instruction (100) is copied from the Program Counter (PC) into the Memory Address Register (MAR).
stages.whatChanges: MAR receives address 100 and places it on the address bus.

stages.title: Fetch 2: Read Instruction & Increment PC
stages.summary: Main memory returns the instruction at address 100 ('LOAD 5') into the MDR while the PC increments to 101.
stages.whatChanges: MDR holds 'LOAD 5'; PC advances to 101 ready for the next instruction.

stages.title: Fetch 3: Transfer MDR to CIR
stages.summary: The fetched instruction is copied from the MDR into the Current Instruction Register (CIR).
stages.whatChanges: CIR now holds 'LOAD 5', freeing MDR for operand data transfers.

stages.title: Decode Instruction
stages.summary: The Control Unit decodes 'LOAD 5' into opcode LOAD (read from memory into ACC) and operand address 5.
stages.whatChanges: Control signals prepare to read data from address 5 (ALU arithmetic is NOT needed for LOAD).

prediction.prompt: Which unit decodes the instruction inside the CIR?
prediction.explanation: The Control Unit decodes the opcode and operand in the CIR and generates control signals.

stages.title: Execute LOAD 5
stages.summary: Memory address 5 returns value 42 into the MDR, which is then loaded into the Accumulator (ACC).
stages.whatChanges: ACC updates from 0 to 42; the CPU is now ready to fetch the next instruction at PC = 101.

pilot4b-sci-water-cycle.title: The Water Cycle (Simplified Pathway)
pilot4b-sci-water-cycle.instructions: Step around this cyclic pathway and observe how water changes state and exchanges heat energy.
pilot4b-sci-water-cycle.fallbackText: Solar heat causes evaporation (liquid to vapour), cooling causes condensation (vapour to droplets forming clouds), gravity drives precipitation, and runoff/infiltration returns water to collection bodies.
pilot4b-sci-water-cycle.modelNote: This 4-stage loop is a simplified pathway within a larger interconnected natural cycle—not every water molecule follows the same four stages in order (some evaporate again immediately or remain in groundwater/glaciers).

stages.title: Evaporation
stages.summary: Thermal energy from the Sun warms surface water in rivers, lakes, and oceans, turning liquid water into invisible water vapour that rises.
stages.whatChanges: Liquid water absorbs heat and changes into gas (water vapour).

stages.title: Condensation
stages.summary: As warm water vapour rises into cooler upper air, it loses thermal energy and condenses into tiny liquid droplets around dust particles, forming clouds.
stages.whatChanges: Water vapour releases heat and turns back into liquid droplets.

stages.title: Precipitation
stages.summary: Cloud droplets combine until they become too heavy to stay suspended, falling to Earth as rain (or hail/snow in cold regions).
stages.whatChanges: Gravity pulls heavy water droplets downward to land and sea.

stages.title: Collection & Runoff
stages.summary: Rainwater flows over land as surface runoff or infiltrates into soil and groundwater, collecting in rivers, lakes, and oceans.
stages.whatChanges: Water returns to surface reservoirs and underground aquifers.

sequenceChallenge.prompt: Order this simplified 4-stage water pathway starting from solar warming of ocean water.
sequenceChallenge.explanation: Evaporation lifts vapour → Condensation forms clouds → Precipitation falls → Collection returns water to reservoirs.

pilot4b-chem-electrolysis.title: Electrolysis of Molten Lead(II) Bromide (Virtual Model)
pilot4b-chem-electrolysis.instructions: Step through how melting frees ions and how opposite electrodes drive concurrent redox reactions.
pilot4b-chem-electrolysis.accessibilityLabel: Electrolysis of molten lead II bromide four-stage stepper
pilot4b-chem-electrolysis.fallbackText: Solid PbBr2 cannot conduct because ions are fixed. Melting frees Pb2+ and Br- ions. Under DC voltage, Pb2+ is reduced to molten lead at the negative cathode while Br- is simultaneously oxidised to brown bromine vapour at the positive anode.
pilot4b-chem-electrolysis.modelNote: Conceptual virtual demonstration only—lead(II) bromide and bromine vapour are toxic and corrosive, so this is NOT an independent student practical (teacher fume-cupboard demonstration only). Cathode reduction and anode oxidation occur concurrently.

stages.title: Solid Ionic Lattice (No Conduction)
stages.summary: At room temperature, Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions are locked in a rigid ionic lattice and cannot move to carry charge.

stages.title: Heating to Melt PbBr₂
stages.summary: Heating above 373 °C melts the solid, breaking the rigid lattice so Pb²⁺ cations and Br⁻ anions move freely.
stages.whatChanges: Free-moving ions make the molten salt an electrical conductor (electrolyte).

stages.title: DC Power Applied: Ion Migration
stages.summary: Applying DC voltage attracts positive Pb²⁺ ions toward the negative cathode and negative Br⁻ ions toward the positive anode.

prediction.prompt: Which ion moves to the positive electrode (anode) and what happens to it?
options: Br⁻ moves to the anode and loses electrons (oxidation)
Pb²⁺ moves to the anode and gains electrons
Br⁻ moves to the cathode and gains electrons
prediction.explanation: Opposites attract: negative Br⁻ ions migrate to the positive anode and lose electrons (oxidation) to form Br₂.

stages.title: Concurrent Cathode & Anode Reactions
stages.summary: Reduction and oxidation occur simultaneously: at the cathode Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (silvery molten lead); at the anode 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (brown bromine vapour).
stages.whyItMatters: Electrons removed at the anode flow through the external circuit to the cathode, balancing charge continuously.

pilot4b-bio-digestion.title: Human Digestion Pathway
pilot4b-bio-digestion.instructions: Step through each organ to distinguish mechanical digestion, chemical digestion, absorption, and egestion.
pilot4b-bio-digestion.fallbackText: Mouth chews food and starts starch digestion (amylase); Stomach churns food with acid and protease; Small Intestine completes chemical digestion and absorbs nutrients via villi; Large Intestine absorbs water; Rectum stores and egests undigested faeces.

stages.title: Mouth (Ingestion & Early Digestion)
stages.summary: Teeth chew food into smaller pieces (mechanical digestion) while salivary amylase begins breaking starch into maltose (chemical digestion).

stages.title: Stomach
stages.summary: Muscular walls churn food (mechanical) while hydrochloric acid kills pathogens and provides acidic pH for pepsin (protease) to begin protein digestion.

stages.title: Small Intestine (Digestion & Absorption)
stages.summary: Bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic and intestinal enzymes complete chemical digestion into glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, and glycerol, which absorb through villi into the bloodstream.

stages.title: Large Intestine (Water Absorption)
stages.summary: Remaining water and mineral ions are absorbed from undigested material, forming semi-solid faeces.

stages.title: Rectum & Anus (Egestion)
stages.summary: Undigested food waste (faeces) is stored in the rectum and expelled through the anus—this is egestion.
stages.commonMisconception: Egestion (removing undigested food) is different from excretion (removing metabolic waste like urea and CO₂).

pilot4b-cs-binary-search.title: Binary Search Trace (Target = 42)
pilot4b-cs-binary-search.instructions: Step through the pointer updates (low, mid, high) as binary search locates 42 inside [4, 11, 18, 25, 33, 42, 57].
pilot4b-cs-binary-search.accessibilityLabel: Binary search four-stage pointer trace stepper
pilot4b-cs-binary-search.fallbackText: Start with low=0, high=6. Mid=3 gives 25 < 42, so set low=4. Next mid=floor((4+6)/2)=5 gives 42 == 42: target found at index 5.
pilot4b-cs-binary-search.modelNote: 0-based indexing on sorted array [4, 11, 18, 25, 33, 42, 57]; integer midpoint convention: mid = floor((low + high) / 2). Terminates when array[mid] == target or low > high (not found).

stages.title: Initialise Search Bounds
stages.summary: Set low = 0 and high = 6 to cover all 7 sorted elements [4, 11, 18, 25, 33, 42, 57].

stages.title: Comparison 1: Inspect mid = 3
stages.summary: Compute mid = floor((0 + 6) / 2) = 3. Compare array[3] = 25 with target 42: since 25 < 42, 42 cannot be in indices 0..3.
stages.whatChanges: Half the array (indices 0..3) is eliminated in one comparison.

stages.title: Narrow Bounds: low ← mid + 1
stages.summary: Move low to mid + 1 = 4 so the active search range becomes indices 4..6 ([33, 42, 57]).

stages.title: Comparison 2: Inspect mid = 5 (Found!)
stages.summary: Compute mid = floor((4 + 6) / 2) = 5. Compare array[5] = 42 with target 42: exact match! Algorithm terminates returning index 5.

pilot4b-math-linear-eq.title: Solving 3x + 5 = 20 (Preserving Equality)
pilot4b-math-linear-eq.instructions: Step through each algebraic transformation and observe how both sides stay equal.
pilot4b-math-linear-eq.fallbackText: Start with 3x + 5 = 20. Subtract 5 from both sides to get 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 5. Substitute back: 3(5) + 5 = 20.

stages.title: Original Equation
stages.summary: We want to isolate x. Currently x is multiplied by 3 and then 5 is added.

stages.title: Subtract 5 from Both Sides
stages.summary: Undo '+ 5' by subtracting 5 from both sides: (3x + 5) − 5 = 20 − 5, giving 3x = 15.
stages.whyItMatters: Subtracting the same value from both sides preserves equality.

stages.title: Divide Both Sides by 3
stages.summary: Undo '× 3' by dividing both sides by 3: 3x / 3 = 15 / 3, giving x = 5.

stages.title: Verify by Substitution
stages.summary: Substitute x = 5 into 3x + 5: 3(5) + 5 = 15 + 5 = 20, matching the right-hand side.

pilot4b-alevel-electrophilic-add.title: Electrophilic Addition of HBr to Ethene
pilot4b-alevel-electrophilic-add.instructions: Step through electron-pair movement, bond breaking/forming, and intermediate formation.
pilot4b-alevel-electrophilic-add.fallbackText: Ethene's C=C pi bond attacks the delta-positive H of polar HBr; the H-Br bond breaks heterolytically to yield an ethyl carbocation (CH3CH2+) and Br-; finally Br- donates a lone pair to the positive carbon to form bromoethane (CH3CH2Br).

stages.title: Polarised Electrophile Approaches π Bond
stages.summary: HBr is permanently polar (Hδ⁺–Brδ⁻) because Br is more electronegative than H. It approaches the high electron density of ethene's C=C π bond.

stages.title: π-Bond Attack & Heterolytic Fission
stages.summary: A pair of electrons from the C=C π bond forms a new C–H σ bond with Hδ⁺. Simultaneously, the H–Br bond breaks heterolytically, sending both bonding electrons onto Br.

reactionMeta.electronMovement: Curly arrow 1: C=C π bond → Hδ⁺; Curly arrow 2: H–Br bond pair → Br.

prediction.prompt: What intermediate ion is formed when the π bond forms a C–H bond and Br⁻ departs?
prediction.explanation: The second carbon loses its share of the π electrons, leaving a positively charged ethyl carbocation (CH₃–CH₂⁺).

stages.title: Carbocation Intermediate & Br⁻ Nucleophile
stages.summary: An unstable, positively charged ethyl carbocation intermediate (CH₃–CH₂⁺) exists briefly alongside the bromide ion (:Br⁻) carrying a lone pair.

stages.title: Nucleophilic Attack → Bromoethane
stages.summary: The bromide ion donates a lone pair of electrons to the positively charged carbon, forming a C–Br covalent bond and yielding saturated bromoethane (CH₃CH₂Br).

reactionMeta.electronMovement: Curly arrow: lone pair on :Br⁻ → positively charged C⁺.

previewStep4cExamples.title: Explore Eukaryotic Animal Cell Organelles
previewStep4cExamples.instructions: Select each numbered hotspot (or use Next Part / the label list) to compare organelle structure and function.
previewStep4cExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive eukaryotic animal cell organelle diagram
previewStep4cExamples.fallbackText: Nucleus stores genetic DNA; Mitochondrion generates ATP via aerobic respiration across folded cristae; Rough ER synthesises and folds proteins via bound ribosomes; Plasma Membrane selectively regulates entry and exit of substances.
previewStep4cExamples.modelNote: Idealised eukaryotic animal cell schematic (not drawn to scale).

diagram.altText: Cross-section diagram of an animal cell with nucleus, mitochondrion, rough endoplasmic reticulum, and plasma membrane
diagram.identifyAltText: Unlabelled schematic animal cell diagram with four numbered regions
diagram.caption: Schematic eukaryotic animal cell.

hotspots.label: Nucleus
hotspots.summary: Control centre containing chromosomal DNA surrounded by a double nuclear envelope with nuclear pores.
hotspots.functionText: Stores genetic instructions and coordinates transcription of mRNA.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Nuclear pores allow mRNA to exit to ribosomes in the cytoplasm—including ribosomes bound to the Rough ER—while protecting DNA inside the nuclear envelope.
hotspots.relationshipExplanation: mRNA transcribed in the nucleus passes through nuclear pores and is translated by ribosomes, including those attached to the Rough ER for secretory and membrane protein synthesis.

hotspots.label: Mitochondrion
hotspots.summary: Double-membraned organelle whose inner membrane folds inward into cristae.
hotspots.functionText: Site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy from glucose—some transferred to ATP for cellular work, and some dissipated as heat.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Folded cristae create a large surface area for electron transport chain enzymes and ATP synthase.

hotspots.label: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum
hotspots.summary: Network of flattened membrane sacs (cisternae) studded with 80S ribosomes.
hotspots.functionText: Synthesises, folds, and transports secretory and membrane proteins.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Bound ribosomes translate mRNA that exited through nuclear pores directly into polypeptides entering the ER lumen for folding.
hotspots.relationshipExplanation: Continuous with the outer nuclear membrane so mRNA passing through nuclear pores rapidly reaches rough ER-associated ribosomes.

hotspots.label: Plasma Membrane
hotspots.summary: Partially permeable phospholipid bilayer with embedded transport and receptor proteins.
hotspots.functionText: Controls movement of ions, nutrients, and waste into and out of the cell.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Hydrophobic fatty-acid tails restrict polar molecules while channel and carrier proteins provide selective pathways.

identifyPrompts.prompt: Select the organelle whose folded inner membrane (cristae) maximises energy transfer to ATP during aerobic respiration.
identifyPrompts.explanation: The mitochondrion (Region 2) carries out aerobic respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O), transferring released energy to ATP across its folded cristae.
identifyPrompts.hintText: Look for the bean-shaped organelle in the upper right.

nonVisualQuestion.prompt: Which animal cell organelle has folded inner membranes (cristae) that maximise surface area for aerobic respiration and ATP synthesis?
nonVisualQuestion.explanation: The mitochondrion has folded cristae hosting electron transport chain enzymes and ATP synthase, transferring energy released during aerobic respiration to ATP.

previewStep4cExamples.title: Mammalian Heart Chambers, Valves & Vessels
previewStep4cExamples.instructions: Explore the chambers and valve in anatomical orientation (as if looking at a person facing you).
previewStep4cExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive mammalian heart chambers and valves diagram
previewStep4cExamples.fallbackText: Right atrium receives deoxygenated blood and passes it to the right ventricle (pumps to lungs). Left atrium receives oxygenated blood from pulmonary veins and passes it through the bicuspid valve to the thick-walled left ventricle, which pumps blood into the aorta.

diagram.altText: Schematic mammalian heart showing right and left atria, right and left ventricles, bicuspid valve, and aorta
diagram.identifyAltText: Unlabelled schematic mammalian heart diagram with six numbered regions
diagram.caption: Anatomical view: right side (deoxygenated, blue) on viewer's left; left side (oxygenated, red) on viewer's right.

hotspots.label: Right Atrium
hotspots.summary: Upper chamber on the anatomical right side receiving deoxygenated blood from the vena cava.
hotspots.relationshipExplanation: Contracts to push deoxygenated blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

hotspots.label: Right Ventricle
hotspots.summary: Lower right chamber pumping deoxygenated blood via the pulmonary artery to the lungs.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Thinner muscular wall than the left ventricle because the lungs are close and require lower pressure.

hotspots.label: Left Atrium
hotspots.summary: Upper left chamber receiving oxygenated blood from the lungs via the pulmonary veins.
hotspots.relationshipExplanation: Passes oxygenated blood through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle.

hotspots.label: Bicuspid (Mitral) Valve
hotspots.summary: Atrioventricular valve between the left atrium and left ventricle.
hotspots.functionText: Prevents backflow of oxygenated blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium when the left ventricle contracts.

hotspots.label: Left Ventricle
hotspots.summary: Thickest-walled chamber of the heart, pumping oxygenated blood into the aorta.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Thick cardiac muscle generates high pressure needed to propel blood around the entire systemic circulation.
hotspots.relationshipExplanation: Ejects oxygenated blood through the aortic semilunar valve directly into the aorta.

hotspots.label: Aorta
hotspots.summary: Largest artery carrying high-pressure oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to body tissues.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Thick elastic walls stretch and recoil to smooth out high-pressure pulses.

identifyPrompts.prompt: Select the valve that prevents backflow of oxygenated blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during ventricular contraction.
identifyPrompts.explanation: The bicuspid (mitral) valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle and prevents backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium.

nonVisualQuestion.prompt: Which heart valve prevents backflow of oxygenated blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium when the left ventricle contracts?
nonVisualQuestion.explanation: The bicuspid (mitral) valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle, closing during ventricular systole to prevent backflow into the left atrium.

previewStep4cExamples.title: Fractional Distillation Laboratory Apparatus
previewStep4cExamples.instructions: Explore each part of the apparatus to see why its position matters for pure separation.
previewStep4cExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive fractional distillation laboratory apparatus diagram
previewStep4cExamples.fallbackText: The round-bottom flask heats the liquid mixture; the fractionating column provides repeated condensation and vaporisation; the thermometer bulb sits level with the side-arm to read vapour boiling point; the Liebig condenser cools vapour (cold water in at the lower end, out at the upper end) into the receiving flask.

diagram.altText: Fractional distillation setup with round-bottom flask, fractionating column, thermometer at side-arm, Liebig condenser, and receiving flask
diagram.identifyAltText: Unlabelled fractional distillation laboratory apparatus diagram with five numbered regions

hotspots.label: Round-Bottom Flask
hotspots.summary: Holds the miscible liquid mixture (e.g. ethanol and water) and anti-bumping granules during heating.

hotspots.label: Fractionating Column
hotspots.summary: Tall glass column packed with glass beads creating a temperature gradient (hotter at bottom, cooler at top).
hotspots.structureToFunction: Provides a large surface area for repeated condensation and re-vaporisation so only the lower-boiling fraction reaches the top.

hotspots.label: Thermometer Bulb (at Side-Arm)
hotspots.summary: Bulb positioned directly opposite the side-arm leading to the condenser.
hotspots.functionText: Measures the exact boiling point of the vapour passing into the condenser.
hotspots.commonMisconception: Never dip the thermometer bulb into the boiling liquid—that reads the mixture temperature, not the distilling vapour.

hotspots.label: Liebig Condenser
hotspots.summary: Water-jacketed tube cooling hot vapour back into liquid distillate.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Cold water enters at the lower inlet and exits at the upper outlet so the jacket stays completely filled for efficient counter-current cooling.

hotspots.label: Receiving Flask
hotspots.summary: Collects the condensed liquid fraction (distillate) cleanly.

identifyPrompts.prompt: Select the component that measures the boiling point of the vapour entering the condenser.
identifyPrompts.explanation: The thermometer bulb is placed level with the side-arm to measure the distilling vapour's exact temperature.

nonVisualQuestion.prompt: In fractional distillation, where should the thermometer bulb be positioned to measure the boiling point of the distilling fraction accurately?
options: Submerged inside the boiling liquid mixture
Level with the side-arm leading into the Liebig condenser
At the lower cold-water inlet of the condenser
nonVisualQuestion.explanation: Positioning the thermometer bulb level with the side-arm measures the exact temperature of the vapour passing into the condenser.

previewStep4cExamples.title: Protein Tertiary Structure & Stabilising Bonds
previewStep4cExamples.instructions: Observe the diagram first, then reveal markers to compare backbone hydrogen bonds with R-group interactions.
previewStep4cExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive protein tertiary structure interactions diagram
previewStep4cExamples.fallbackText: Secondary structures (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets) are stabilised by peptide backbone hydrogen bonds. Tertiary 3D folding is stabilised by R-group interactions: strong covalent disulfide bridges (between cysteine residues), ionic bonds (sensitive to pH), hydrogen bonds, and hydrophobic interactions clustering non-polar R-groups inward. Not all proteins contain disulfide bridges or quaternary structure.
previewStep4cExamples.modelNote: Not all proteins contain disulfide bridges (only those with appropriately positioned cysteine R-groups), and monomeric proteins have tertiary structure without quaternary structure. Disulfide bridges are covalent bonds, whereas hydrogen bonds (between polar R-groups), ionic bonds, and hydrophobic interactions are non-covalent.

diagram.altText: Schematic regions representing alpha-helix, beta-pleated sheet, disulfide bridge, ionic bond, and hydrophobic core in a folded protein

hotspots.label: α-Helix (Backbone H-Bonds)
hotspots.summary: Regular coiled secondary structure stabilised by non-covalent hydrogen bonds between peptide backbone C=O and N–H groups (four residues apart).
hotspots.commonMisconception: Secondary structure relies on peptide backbone H-bonds, whereas hydrogen bonds between polar R-groups can also contribute to tertiary structure.

hotspots.label: β-Pleated Sheet (Backbone H-Bonds)
hotspots.summary: Folded sheet formed by non-covalent hydrogen bonding between parallel or antiparallel polypeptide backbone strands.

hotspots.label: Disulfide Bridge (R-Group Covalent)
hotspots.summary: Strong covalent S–S bond formed by oxidation between two cysteine thiol (–SH) R-groups (unlike non-covalent H-bonds, ionic, and hydrophobic interactions).
hotspots.commonMisconception: Not all proteins have disulfide bonds; they occur mainly where cysteine residues align closely (e.g. insulin, antibodies).

hotspots.label: Ionic & R-Group H-Bond Interactions
hotspots.summary: Non-covalent tertiary interactions: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ionised R-groups (e.g. –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻) alongside hydrogen bonds between polar R-groups.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Sensitive to pH and temperature: extreme pH disrupts ionic bonds while excess heat breaks weak R-group hydrogen bonds, denaturing active sites.

hotspots.label: Hydrophobic Core (Non-Polar R-Groups)
hotspots.summary: Non-polar R-groups cluster inward away from surrounding aqueous cytoplasm while hydrophilic R-groups face outward.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Drives compact globular folding and keeps water-soluble enzymes soluble in blood or cytosol.

previewStep4cExamples.title: Identify Organic Functional Groups
previewStep4cExamples.instructions: Select each molecule to inspect its functional group, polarity, and characteristic reaction.
previewStep4cExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive organic chemistry functional groups diagram
previewStep4cExamples.fallbackText: Ethene (H2C=CH2) has an electron-rich C=C alkene double bond; Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) has a polar hydroxyl -OH group; Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) has an acidic carboxyl -COOH group; Methylamine (CH3NH2) has a basic amino -NH2 group with a nitrogen lone pair.
previewStep4cExamples.modelNote: Panels show condensed structural formulae (grouping C–H bonds as CH₃, CH₂, etc.); fully displayed formulae draw every individual covalent bond explicitly (including every C–H, O–H, and C=O bond).

diagram.altText: Four panels showing condensed structural formulae for ethene, ethanol, ethanoic acid, and methylamine
diagram.identifyAltText: Four panels showing four numbered organic molecules in condensed structural formula form

hotspots.label: Alkene (C=C Double Bond)
hotspots.summary: Unsaturated hydrocarbon containing a σ bond and an exposed, electron-rich π bond.
hotspots.structureToFunction: High π-electron density attracts electrophiles, undergoing electrophilic addition.

hotspots.label: Alcohol Hydroxyl (–OH)
hotspots.summary: Polar O–H bond capable of forming hydrogen bonds with water.

hotspots.label: Carboxylic Acid (–COOH)
hotspots.summary: Combines C=O and –OH on the same carbon; acts as a weak Brønsted–Lowry acid.

hotspots.label: Primary Amine (–NH₂)
hotspots.summary: Nitrogen carries a lone pair of electrons, acting as both a weak base and nucleophile.

identifyPrompts.prompt: Select the molecule containing the weak-acid carboxyl functional group (–COOH).
identifyPrompts.explanation: Ethanoic acid (condensed formula CH₃–COOH) contains the carboxyl group –COOH (a C=O and –OH attached to the same carbon).

nonVisualQuestion.prompt: Which condensed structural formula represents a carboxylic acid containing the weak-acid –COOH functional group?
nonVisualQuestion.explanation: CH₃–COOH (ethanoic acid) contains the carboxyl group (–COOH), which partially dissociates in water to release H⁺ ions.

previewStep4cExamples.title: Von Neumann CPU Architecture Explorer
previewStep4cExamples.instructions: Select each hardware block to trace its role and how it connects to neighbouring blocks.
previewStep4cExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive Von Neumann CPU architecture diagram
previewStep4cExamples.fallbackText: Control Unit fetches and decodes instructions; ALU runs arithmetic and logic; Registers hold fast working values (PC, MAR, MDR, CIR, ACC); System Buses (address, data, control) link CPU to Main Memory (RAM).
previewStep4cExamples.modelNote: Simplified curriculum Von Neumann model: bus directions (unidirectional address bus, bidirectional data bus) reflect standard GCSE/IGCSE/A-Level teaching conventions rather than all modern multiplexed or DMA hardware designs.

diagram.altText: Block diagram of a Von Neumann CPU showing Control Unit, ALU, Registers, System Buses, and Main Memory

hotspots.label: Control Unit (CU)
hotspots.summary: Coordinates fetch–decode–execute timing and sends control signals across the control bus.
hotspots.relationshipExplanation: Reads the decoded instruction from CIR (in Registers) and issues read/write signals on the control bus.

hotspots.label: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)
hotspots.summary: Executes integer arithmetic (+, −) and Boolean logic operations (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons).
hotspots.relationshipExplanation: Stores calculation results directly into the Accumulator register.

hotspots.label: CPU Registers (PC, MAR, MDR, CIR, ACC)
hotspots.summary: Ultra-fast small storage locations inside the CPU holding current addresses, instructions, and intermediate data.

hotspots.label: System Buses (Address, Data, Control)
hotspots.summary: In the simplified curriculum model, parallel electrical pathways carry memory addresses (unidirectional from CPU to memory), data/instructions (bidirectional), and control/timing signals.

hotspots.label: Main Memory (RAM)
hotspots.summary: Volatile primary memory holding both currently running program instructions and working data.

previewStep4cExamples.title: Ammeter vs Voltmeter Connection Explorer
previewStep4cExamples.instructions: Inspect each component in the test circuit to understand why ammeters and voltmeters are wired differently.
previewStep4cExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive electrical circuit with ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel
previewStep4cExamples.fallbackText: The ammeter is connected in series with the resistor so the same current flows through it (very low internal resistance). The voltmeter is connected in parallel across the resistor to measure potential difference without drawing significant current (very high internal resistance).

diagram.altText: Circuit diagram showing cell, ammeter connected in series, resistor, and voltmeter connected in parallel across the resistor
diagram.identifyAltText: Circuit diagram with four numbered components in series and parallel positions

hotspots.label: DC Cell / Power Supply
hotspots.summary: Provides electromotive force (e.m.f.) to drive electric charge around the closed loop.

hotspots.label: Ammeter (Connected in Series)
hotspots.summary: Measures electric current (I) in amperes (A) flowing through the circuit.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Very low internal resistance ensures it does not significantly reduce the current being measured.

hotspots.label: Test Resistor (R)
hotspots.summary: Component whose resistance opposes current flow and across which potential difference is measured.

hotspots.label: Voltmeter (Connected in Parallel)
hotspots.summary: Measures potential difference (V) in volts (V) across the ends of the resistor.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Very high internal resistance prevents current from bypassing the resistor through the voltmeter.
hotspots.commonMisconception: Connecting a voltmeter in series blocks current because of its very high resistance.

identifyPrompts.prompt: Select the instrument connected in PARALLEL with very high internal resistance.
identifyPrompts.explanation: The voltmeter is connected in parallel across the resistor to measure potential difference without drawing significant current.

nonVisualQuestion.prompt: Which electrical measuring instrument is connected in PARALLEL across a component and has very high internal resistance?
nonVisualQuestion.explanation: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across a component and has very high internal resistance so negligible current bypasses the component.

previewStep4cExamples.title: Idealised Soil Profile Horizons
previewStep4cExamples.instructions: Select each horizon from top to bottom to compare texture, humus content, and role in plant growth.
previewStep4cExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive idealised soil profile horizons diagram
previewStep4cExamples.fallbackText: O Horizon: surface organic leaf litter. A Horizon (Topsoil): dark, humus-rich layer where most plant roots and earthworms live. B Horizon (Subsoil): denser clay and leached minerals. C Horizon: partially weathered parent rock fragments. R Horizon: unweathered solid bedrock.
previewStep4cExamples.modelNote: Represents an idealised mature soil profile (O–A–B–C–R). Real soils vary widely with climate, erosion, and agriculture—not all soils contain every horizon.

diagram.altText: Vertical soil profile cross-section showing five horizontal bands labelled O, A, B, C, and R from top to bottom

hotspots.label: O Horizon (Organic Layer)
hotspots.summary: Surface layer of fallen leaves, twigs, and decomposing organic litter.

hotspots.label: A Horizon (Topsoil)
hotspots.summary: Dark, fertile mixture of mineral particles and humus supporting most crop roots and soil microbes.
hotspots.structureToFunction: Rich humus retains moisture and nutrients while crumb structure allows air circulation to roots.

hotspots.label: B Horizon (Subsoil)
hotspots.summary: Lighter, denser layer accumulating clay and minerals leached downward from topsoil.

hotspots.label: C Horizon (Weathered Parent Rock)
hotspots.summary: Partially broken-down rock fragments with very little organic matter.

hotspots.label: R Horizon (Bedrock)
hotspots.summary: Continuous, unweathered solid rock beneath the soil profile.

previewStep4dExamples.title: Balance the Formation of Water
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Use the + and − buttons to set whole-number coefficients so hydrogen and oxygen atoms are conserved in the simplest ratio.
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive chemical equation balancer for water formation
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: Balanced equation: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) (4 H atoms and 2 O atoms on both sides).

prediction.prompt: One molecule of O₂ provides 2 oxygen atoms. How many H₂O molecules must be formed to use both oxygen atoms?
prediction.explanation: Each H₂O contains 1 oxygen atom, so 2 H₂O molecules balance 1 O₂ molecule.

previewStep4dExamples.successExplanation: Balanced! 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) conserves 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms in the simplest whole-number ratio (2 : 1 : 2).

previewStep4dExamples.title: Balance the Haber Process Equation
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Balance nitrogen and hydrogen atoms across the reversible reaction arrow.
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive chemical equation balancer for the Haber process
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: Balanced equation: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (2 N atoms and 6 H atoms on both sides).
previewStep4dExamples.modelNote: Atom conservation verifies stoichiometry only; actual industrial ammonia synthesis requires an iron catalyst, ~450 °C, and ~200 atm.
previewStep4dExamples.successExplanation: Balanced! N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) conserves 2 N atoms and 6 H atoms in the simplest ratio (1 : 3 : 2).

previewStep4dExamples.title: Balance Ca(OH)₂ + HCl Neutralisation
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Remember that Ca(OH)₂ has 2 O atoms and 2 H atoms. Balance all four elements.
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive chemical equation balancer for calcium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: Balanced equation: Ca(OH)₂(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l) (1 Ca, 2 O, 4 H, 2 Cl on both sides).
hints: Start by balancing chlorine (Cl) on both sides, then check total hydrogen and oxygen.
previewStep4dExamples.successExplanation: Balanced! Ca(OH)₂(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l) conserves Ca, O, H, and Cl.

previewStep4dExamples.title: Balance the Anode Oxidation Half-Equation
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Balance both bromine atoms and net electric charge using Br⁻, Br₂, and electrons (e⁻).
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive ionic half-equation balancer for bromide oxidation
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: Balanced half-equation: 2Br⁻(l) → Br₂(g) + 2e⁻ (2 Br atoms and −2 total charge on each side).
previewStep4dExamples.modelNote: Represents the anode oxidation half-equation during electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide (PbBr₂) at high temperature (~370–400 °C), well above bromine's boiling point (58.8 °C), which is why bromine is evolved as a brown gas Br₂(g) rather than liquid Br₂(l).
previewStep4dExamples.successExplanation: Balanced! 2Br⁻(l) → Br₂(g) + 2e⁻ conserves 2 Br atoms and a net electric charge of −2 on each side.

previewStep4dExamples.title: Build a 12 V Series Two-Lamp Circuit
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Close the switch and place two 6 Ω lamps in Series Slots 1 and 2 so main current is 1.00 A and Lamp 1 reads 6.00 V.
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive 12 volt DC series electrical circuit builder
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: With a closed switch and two 6 Ω lamps in series on a 12 V supply, R_eq = 12 Ω, I = 1.00 A, and each lamp has 6.00 V across it (P = 6.00 W).

goal.description: 2 lamps in series, I_total = 1.00 A, V across Slot 1 = 6.00 V

previewStep4dExamples.successExplanation: Verified! Two 6 Ω lamps in series give R_eq = 12 Ω, so I = 12 V / 12 Ω = 1.00 A and each lamp receives 6.00 V (KVL: 6 V + 6 V = 12 V).

previewStep4dExamples.title: Build a 6 V Parallel Two-Lamp Circuit
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Place a 6 Ω lamp in Branch A and a 6 Ω lamp in Branch B so each branch draws 1.00 A and total current is 2.00 A.
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive 6 volt DC parallel electrical circuit builder
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: With two 6 Ω lamps in parallel across 6 V, each branch draws 1.00 A, total current is 2.00 A, and equivalent resistance is 3.00 Ω.

goal.description: Two 6 Ω lamps in parallel (I_A = 1.00 A, I_B = 1.00 A, I_total = 2.00 A)

previewStep4dExamples.successExplanation: Verified! Both 6 Ω parallel branches receive 6.00 V, each draws 1.00 A, and KCL holds: I_total = 1.00 A + 1.00 A = 2.00 A (R_eq = 3.00 Ω).

previewStep4dExamples.title: Mixed Series-Parallel Reference Circuit (12 V · 2 Ω + 6 Ω ∥ 6 Ω)
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Place a 2 Ω resistor in the main series loop and two 6 Ω resistors in parallel Branches A and B, then verify R_eq = 5.00 Ω, I_total = 2.40 A, V_parallel = 7.20 V, and I_A = I_B = 1.20 A.
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive 12 volt mixed series-parallel electrical circuit builder
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: In a 12 V mixed circuit with a 2 Ω series resistor feeding two parallel 6 Ω resistors, R_parallel = 3 Ω, R_eq = 5 Ω, I_total = 2.40 A, V_series = 4.80 V, V_parallel = 7.20 V, and each parallel branch carries 1.20 A.

goal.description: R_eq = 5.00 Ω, I_total = 2.40 A, V_parallel = 7.20 V, I_A = I_B = 1.20 A

previewStep4dExamples.successExplanation: Verified! R_parallel = 3.00 Ω + 2.00 Ω series = 5.00 Ω total; I_total = 2.40 A splits evenly (1.20 A each) across the parallel 6 Ω branches at 7.20 V (KVL: 4.80 V + 7.20 V = 12.00 V).

previewStep4dExamples.title: Fix the Short Circuit & Meter Misconnection
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: The starting circuit has a plain wire shorting Branch B and a misplaced ammeter in the parallel probe. Replace Branch B with a 6 Ω resistor and place the Voltmeter in the parallel probe.

goal.description: Eliminate short circuit & meter faults (I_total = 2.00 A, V_probe = 6.00 V)

previewStep4dExamples.successExplanation: Faults resolved! Both branches now have safe 6 Ω loads, the ammeter is in series (2.00 A), and the voltmeter is in parallel (6.00 V).

previewStep4dExamples.title: Build the Antiparallel Complementary DNA Strand

previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive DNA complementary base pairing builder
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: DNA template 3′-TAC GGA-5′ pairs with complementary 5′-ATG CCT-3′ (A–T has 2 H-bonds, C–G has 3 H-bonds).
previewStep4dExamples.modelNote: Shows a 6-base DNA fragment; strands run antiparallel (3′→5′ paired with 5′→3′).

previewStep4dExamples.title: Transcribe 5′→3′ mRNA from the 3′→5′ DNA Template
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Build the complementary mRNA strand. Notice how the coding (non-template) DNA strand would have T where mRNA has U.
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive DNA to mRNA transcription sequence builder
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: DNA template 3′-TAC GAA-5′ transcribes to 5′-AUG CUU-3′ mRNA (coding strand would be 5′-ATG CTT-3′).
previewStep4dExamples.modelNote: RNA polymerase uses the 3′→5′ DNA template (antisense) strand to build 5′→3′ mRNA; the opposite 5′→3′ DNA strand is the coding (sense) strand.

previewStep4dExamples.title: Translate mRNA Codons into a Polypeptide
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Use the standard genetic code: AUG = Met, GGA = Gly, UUU = Phe, UAA = STOP (termination signal, no amino acid).
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive mRNA translation and amino acid sequence builder
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: 5′-AUG GGA UUU UAA-3′ translates to N-Met–Gly–Phe-C (2 condensation peptide bonds) and terminates at the UAA STOP codon.
previewStep4dExamples.modelNote: Complete short coding sequence from AUG start codon to UAA stop codon. In simplified textbook stoichiometry, peptide bond formation is written as a condensation reaction between –COOH and –NH₂ releasing H₂O; in living cells during ribosome-mediated translation, amino acids are first activated onto tRNA (using ATP) and peptidyl transferase in the ribosome catalyses peptide bond formation between aminoacyl-tRNA and peptidyl-tRNA.

previewStep4dExamples.title: Construct the Tt × Tt Monohybrid Punnett Grid
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Select each square in the 2×2 grid and choose the offspring diploid genotype formed by the row and column gametes.
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive monohybrid Punnett square builder for Tt by Tt cross
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: Tt × Tt yields genotype probabilities 25% TT, 50% Tt, 25% tt and phenotype probability 75% tall : 25% dwarf under complete dominance.
previewStep4dExamples.modelNote: Assumes a single autosomal gene with complete dominance (T = tall dominant over t = dwarf recessive) and independent gamete segregation.

previewStep4dExamples.title: Build X = A AND (NOT B) (Declarative JSON Circuit)
previewStep4dExamples.instructions: Add and wire gates so the live truth table matches Target X = [0, 0, 1, 0] for (A,B) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1).
previewStep4dExamples.accessibilityLabel: Interactive declarative Boolean logic circuit builder for A AND NOT B
previewStep4dExamples.fallbackText: Target X = A AND (NOT B): invert B with a NOT gate (G1), then feed A and G1 into an AND gate (G2). Outputs 1 only when A=1 and B=0.

circuitConfig.successExplanation: Functionally equivalent! Your circuit outputs X = 1 exclusively when A = 1 and B = 0.
